title: Spaghetti alle vongole
subtitle: Spaghetti with clams, garlic, white wine, and parsley
excerpt: Spaghetti alle vongole is the Neapolitan clam pasta that rewards a hot pan and a quick hand. Clams open in minutes and release a salty, briny liquor that becomes the sauce. The whole dish takes no longer than it takes to boil the pasta, and it should taste of the sea.
sourceNotes: Classic Neapolitan coastal recipe. Methods drawn from Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992), and traditional vongole preparations documented in the Gambero Rosso guides to Italian regional cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian word for clams, specifically the small venus clam (Venerupis decussata) used in this pasta; in Italy the dish is always made with live clams in their shells.
Soaking live clams or mussels in cold salted water for 20 to 30 minutes so they expel any grit or sand trapped inside the shells.

content.text: Spaghetti alle vongole is a clam pasta from the Neapolitan coast: live
vongole

cooked in a hot, garlicky pan with white wine until they snap open and release their briny liquor. The liquor, the wine, and the starchy pasta water make the sauce with no further work. The clams need
purging
before cooking; do this as soon as you get them home.
Speed matters at the stove. The clams open fast and overcook quickly. Have the pasta nearly done before you add the clams to the pan, and toss everything together in the last 2 minutes.
What you need

items.prepNote: live, in shell, purged in cold salted water for 30 minutes
or one small fresh red chilli, thinly sliced

content.text: Buy live clams from a fishmonger or supermarket fish counter on the day you plan to cook them. Tap any open ones on the counter: if they close, they are alive; discard any that stay open. Discard any that do not open during cooking.
Method
Purge and check the clams

Put {{clams}} of clams into a large bowl of cold water with a generous handful of salt. Leave for 30 minutes. They will open slightly and spit out any grit. Lift them out by hand into a colander; don't tip the bowl or the grit goes back onto the clams. Rinse briefly under cold water.
Cook the pasta
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to the boil. Cook {{pasta-dried}} of spaghetti until 2 minutes short of al dente. Reserve a large mug of pasta water before draining.
Cook the clams and finish

While the pasta cooks, heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a wide frying pan over high heat. Add {{garlic}} of sliced garlic and the chilli flakes if using. Cook for 1 minute until the garlic is fragrant but not coloured.

Tip in the clams and pour in {{dry-white-wine}} of dry white wine. Cover the pan with a lid or a large plate. Cook over high heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan every minute, until nearly all the clams are open. Remove the lid and discard any that remain firmly shut.

Add the drained spaghetti to the clam pan. Toss over high heat for 2 minutes, adding splashes of pasta water to bring the sauce together into a loose, glossy coating. Add the parsley, toss once more, and serve immediately. Lemon wedges on the side.

items.cause: Not purged long enough, or the soaking bowl was tipped rather than the clams being lifted out.
items.fix: Always lift clams out of the soaking water. Rinse again under cold running water. Purge for the full 30 minutes next time.

items.symptom: Sauce is too thin and watery
items.cause: Too much pasta water was added, or the clam liquor wasn't given time to reduce.
items.fix: Let the sauce simmer in the pan without the pasta for 2 minutes before adding the spaghetti, or toss over higher heat for longer.

items.cause: Cooked for too long after opening.
items.fix: As soon as the shells open, the clam meat is done. Add the pasta immediately and work fast. Total time in the pan should not exceed 5 to 6 minutes.

items.cause: Heat too high or garlic added too early without the clams ready to go in.
items.fix: Have everything at hand before you start: purged clams in a bowl, wine measured, pasta nearly cooked. The garlic step only needs 60 seconds.

content.text: Variations

In bianco (without tomato) is the classic. The rosso version adds a spoonful of tomato passata to the pan with the wine. Linguine is the other traditional pasta choice. Some cooks add a small knob of butter at the end to soften the edge of the sauce.
Where this dish lives

Vongole is as Neapolitan as pizza, found in trattorie all along the Campanian coast from Pozzuoli to Paestum. It is also the dish most abused in bad Italian restaurants, where it arrives watery and gritty. Made properly, with live clams and speed at the stove, it stands among the best pasta dishes in Italy. The rule the Neapolitans follow is the same as for all shellfish pasta: the sea itself should provide the seasoning.
